issues.legal_issue: A property provided as a source of income for religious charities is only partially dedicated when the grant does not dedicate the property itself to charity, and its alienation remains valid subject to the charitable obligation.
material_facts: A partition deed expressly described certain separate properties as allotted for charity, but did not describe the disputed property that way; it instead directed that the property be administered by a family member.
The deed required family members to use the property’s income and their own funds to meet the expenses of specified religious charities.
At the time of the partition, the property’s income was insufficient to meet those expenses.
The property was later sold, and the purchasers were sued for a declaration that it belonged absolutely to a trust and that the alienations were invalid.
issues.conclusion: The disputed property was not absolutely dedicated to the temple or a trust. It remained private property subject to a charge to perform the specified charities, and its alienation was valid subject to that obligation.
issues.legal_principle: Whether a religious endowment is absolute or partial depends primarily on the terms of the grant. An express endowment is determined from its terms; an implied endowment is determined by construing the document as a whole. Clear and unambiguous wording governs, while ambiguity may require consideration of the grant’s scheme and language, surrounding circumstances, subsequent dealings, the parties’ conduct, and long usage. A complete dedication creates a trust in favour of the charity; a partial dedication leaves the property’s private character intact but attaches a charge for the charity that follows the property. The Court applied Sree Sree Ishwer Sridhar Jew v. Sushila Bala Dasi, Menakuru Dasaratharami Reddi v. Duddukuru Subba Rao, and Ramkishore Lal v. Kamal Narain, and also considered the authorities discussed in its judgment, including Sri Sri Iswari Bhubaneswari Thakurani v. Brojo Nath Dey and Gopal Lal Sett v. Purna Chandra Basak. No statutory provision was relied on.

predicates.claim_seeks_absolute_charitable_ownershi: The proceeding seeks to establish that property belongs absolutely to a charitable or religious institution and to invalidate its alienation.
predicates.grant_expressly_allots_other_property_fo: The grant expressly identifies property other than the disputed property as allotted for charitable purposes.
predicates.disputed_property_not_expressly_allotted: The grant refers to the disputed property in connection with charitable obligations but does not expressly allot it for charity.
predicates.charity_expenses_must_be_supplemented_fr: The grant requires the responsible private persons to use their own funds if the property income does not cover the charitable expenses.
predicates.property_income_insufficient_at_grant: The property’s income was insufficient to meet the charitable expenses when the grant was made.
predicates.property_remains_private_subject_to_char: The property remains private and may be alienated, but the charitable obligation continues to burden it.

issues.definition: When a claim to absolute charitable ownership and invalid alienation concerns property that the grant did not expressly allot for charity, while requiring private persons to supplement insufficient income from their own funds, the property remains private, may be alienated, and remains subject to the charitable charge.
